name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Preparation steps of potassium dichromate from ore

questiontext.text:
Potassium dichromate (\(\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7\)) is manufactured industrially from chromite ore (\(\text{FeCr}_2\text{O}_4\)). Arrange the following operational steps in the correct chronological sequence:

  1. Fusion of chromite ore with sodium carbonate in free access of air to produce sodium chromate.
  2. Extraction of the fused mass with water and filtration to separate insoluble iron(III) oxide from yellow sodium chromate solution.
  3. Acidification of the yellow sodium chromate solution with sulphuric acid to obtain orange sodium dichromate.
  4. Treatment of the sodium dichromate solution with potassium chloride to crystallise potassium dichromate.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The industrial synthesis of potassium dichromate utilizes chromite ore (\(\text{FeCr}_2\text{O}_4\)) as the starting raw material, proceeding via initial conversion to soluble sodium chromate, subsequent conversion to sodium dichromate by acid, and finally metathesis to less soluble potassium dichromate.

Step 2: Alkaline Oxidative Fusion
Finely powdered chromite ore is fused with sodium carbonate (\(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\)) in a reverberatory furnace in excess air to oxidize chromium from +3 to +6:
\[4\text{FeCr}_2\text{O}_4 + 8\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + 7\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 8\text{Na}_2\text{CrO}_4 + 2\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 8\text{CO}_2\]

Step 3: Extraction and Filtration
The roasted mass is extracted with water. Sodium chromate dissolves completely to give a yellow solution, while iron(III) oxide remains as an insoluble residue and is filtered off.

Step 4: Acidification to Dichromate
The yellow sodium chromate filtrate is acidified with concentrated sulphuric acid, converting chromate into orange sodium dichromate:
\[2\text{Na}_2\text{CrO}_4 + 2\text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 2\text{Na}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O}\]

Step 5: Metathesis with Potassium Chloride and Final Answer
Because sodium dichromate is highly soluble and deliquescent, it is treated with potassium chloride. Potassium dichromate is much less soluble in cold water and precipitates out as orange crystals:
\[\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 2\text{KCl} \rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 2\text{NaCl}\]
Therefore, the correct chronological sequence is oxidative fusion of chromite ore with sodium carbonate, followed by extraction and filtration, followed by acidification to produce sodium dichromate, and concluded by treatment with potassium chloride to crystallise potassium dichromate (\(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Thermodynamic stages of metal cation hydration process

questiontext.text:
The thermochemical transformation of a transition metal from its standard solid state, \(\text{M(s)}\), to its hydrated divalent cation, \(\text{M}^{2+}\text{(aq)}\), is governed by a Born-Haber energy cycle. Arrange the energetic stages of this process in the correct logical sequence:

  1. Sublimation/atomisation of the solid metal into individual gaseous atoms: \(\text{M(s)} \rightarrow \text{M(g)}\)
  2. First ionisation of the gaseous metal atom to produce a gaseous unipositive cation: \(\text{M(g)} \rightarrow \text{M}^+\text{(g)} + \text{e}^-\)
  3. Second ionisation of the unipositive cation to produce a gaseous dipositive cation: \(\text{M}^+\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{M}^{2+}\text{(g)} + \text{e}^-\)
  4. Hydration of the dipositive gaseous cation by solvent water molecules: \(\text{M}^{2+}\text{(g)} + \text{aq} \rightarrow \text{M}^{2+}\text{(aq)}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The standard reduction potential \(E^\circ(\text{M}^{2+}/\text{M})\) of a transition metal depends on the overall enthalpy change for transforming \(\text{M(s)}\) into \(\text{M}^{2+}\text{(aq)}\). In the thermochemical cycle, metallic bonds must first be broken, then electrons are removed sequentially, and finally the resulting gaseous cation interacts with water.

Step 2: Sublimation Stage
The solid metal crystal lattice must first absorb enthalpy of atomisation (\(\Delta_a H^\circ\)) to produce separated gaseous neutral atoms:
\[\text{M(s)} \rightarrow \text{M(g)}\]

Step 3: Successive Ionisation Stages
The isolated gaseous atom loses its outermost electrons one by one. The first ionisation requires the first ionisation enthalpy (\(\Delta_i H^\circ_1\)):
\[\text{M(g)} \rightarrow \text{M}^+\text{(g)} + \text{e}^-\]
Next, removal of the second electron requires the second ionisation enthalpy (\(\Delta_i H^\circ_2\)):
\[\text{M}^+\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{M}^{2+}\text{(g)} + \text{e}^-\]

Step 4: Hydration Stage and Final Answer
The gaseous divalent cation \(\text{M}^{2+}\text{(g)}\) is then solvated by water molecules, releasing hydration enthalpy (\(\Delta_{\text{hyd}} H^\circ\)):
\[\text{M}^{2+}\text{(g)} + \text{aq} \rightarrow \text{M}^{2+}\text{(aq)}\]
Hence, the correct logical progression of energetic stages is atomisation of solid metal, followed by first ionisation, second ionisation, and concluding with hydration of the gaseous divalent cation (\(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q03 - Commercial preparation steps of potassium permanganate

questiontext.text:
Commercial manufacturing of potassium permanganate (\(\text{KMnO}_4\)) from pyrolusite ore (\(\text{MnO}_2\)) involves alkaline oxidative fusion followed by electrochemical oxidation. Arrange the following industrial steps in the correct chronological sequence:

  1. Alkaline oxidative fusion of pyrolusite ore (\(\text{MnO}_2\)) with molten potassium hydroxide in the presence of air or \(\text{KNO}_3\).
  2. Dissolution and extraction of the fused mass to obtain an alkaline dark green solution of potassium manganate (\(\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4\)).
  3. Electrolytic oxidation of the green manganate(VI) solution at the anode to form purple permanganate(VII).
  4. Evaporation and crystallisation to separate dark purple crystals of potassium permanganate (\(\text{KMnO}_4\)).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The industrial synthesis of potassium permanganate proceeds by first converting insoluble manganese dioxide (\(\text{MnO}_2\), oxidation state +4) into soluble potassium manganate (\(\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4\), oxidation state +6) by oxidative alkaline fusion, and subsequently converting manganate(VI) into permanganate (\(\text{KMnO}_4\), oxidation state +7) via anodic oxidation.

Step 2: Oxidative Alkaline Fusion
Finely ground \(\text{MnO}_2\) is fused with \(\text{KOH}\) in the presence of atmospheric oxygen or an oxidizing agent such as \(\text{KNO}_3\):
\[2\text{MnO}_2 + 4\text{KOH} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\]

Step 3: Extraction of Green Manganate
The fused mass is leached with water to dissolve the dark green potassium manganate (\(\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4\)), yielding an intensely green alkaline solution of \(\text{MnO}_4^{2-}\) ions.

Step 4: Electrolytic Oxidation and Crystallisation
The alkaline manganate(VI) solution is electrolyzed in an electrolytic cell with iron electrodes. At the anode, manganate is oxidized to permanganate:
\[\text{MnO}_4^{2-} \rightarrow \text{MnO}_4^- + \text{e}^-\]
Following electrolysis, the resulting purple solution is concentrated by evaporation, and \(\text{KMnO}_4\) crystallises out as almost black, dark purple crystals.

Step 5: Final Answer
The proper chronological sequence of operations is oxidative fusion with potassium hydroxide, followed by extraction of the green manganate solution, subsequent electrolytic oxidation to permanganate, and final crystallisation of potassium permanganate crystals (\(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q04 - Catalytic reaction steps of iron ions with persulphate

questiontext.text:
Transition metal ions exhibit catalytic activity due to their ability to change oxidation states. For the iron(III)-catalysed reaction between iodide and persulphate ions, \(2\text{I}^- + \text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-} \xrightarrow{\text{Fe}^{3+}} \text{I}_2 + 2\text{SO}_4^{2-}\), arrange the elementary redox stages in their correct chronological sequence:

  1. Encounter and collision between aqueous \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) catalyst ions and iodide (\(\text{I}^-\)) reactant ions.
  2. Reduction of \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) to \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) accompanied by the oxidation of iodide ions to molecular iodine (\(\text{I}_2\)).
  3. Interaction of the intermediate \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) ions with peroxodisulphate ions (\(\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}\)).
  4. Re-oxidation of \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) back to \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) accompanied by the reduction of peroxodisulphate to sulphate ions (\(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\)).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The uncatalysed direct reaction between iodide (\(\text{I}^-\)) and peroxodisulphate (\(\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}\)) is kinetically slow due to electrostatic repulsion between two negative ions. Iron(III) facilitates the reaction by providing an alternative two-step pathway with lower activation energy involving the \(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}\) redox couple.

Step 2: First Redox Stage
In the initial stage, \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) cations interact with \(\text{I}^-\) anions. Iron(III) oxidises iodide to elemental iodine while itself being reduced to iron(II):
\[2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{I}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{I}_2\]

Step 3: Second Redox Stage
In the subsequent stage, the generated \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) cations interact with peroxodisulphate anions (\(\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}\)). Iron(II) is re-oxidised back to iron(III), while reducing peroxodisulphate to sulphate:
\[2\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{SO}_4^{2-}\]

Step 4: Catalyst Regeneration and Final Answer
Because \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) is regenerated in the second stage, it becomes available to react with fresh iodide ions, completing the catalytic cycle. Thus, the operational sequence is collision of iron(III) with iodide, reduction to iron(II) forming iodine, encounter of iron(II) with persulphate, and re-oxidation to iron(III) with formation of sulphate (\(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q05 - Heterogeneous catalysis stages on transition metal surfaces

questiontext.text:
Transition metals serve as effective solid catalysts in industrial processes (such as Haber's process or hydrogenation of fats). Arrange the fundamental surface stages of heterogeneous catalysis on a solid transition metal in the correct chronological sequence:

  1. Diffusion of reactant molecules to the catalyst surface and chemisorption on active surface metal sites.
  2. Formation of coordinate chemical bonds between reactant molecules and transition metal atoms using \(3d\) and \(4s\) electrons.
  3. Weakening of existing covalent bonds within the adsorbed reactant molecules and formation of active intermediate complexes (lowering activation energy).
  4. Desorption of the resulting product molecules from the metal surface, freeing active sites for fresh reactants.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In heterogeneous catalysis on transition metal surfaces, catalytic activity arises from the availability of unfilled or partially filled \((n-1)d\) orbitals and outermost \(ns\) orbitals which form temporary chemical bonds with approaching reactant molecules.

Step 2: Adsorption and Bond Formation
The reactant molecules first diffuse to the metal boundary and adsorb onto active surface sites. Surface metal atoms utilize their \(3d\) and \(4s\) electrons to establish temporary bonds with the adsorbate molecules.

Step 3: Intermediate Formation and Reaction
The formation of these surface bonds increases the local concentration of reactants at the catalyst surface and weakens the internal bonds in the reacting molecules, thereby significantly decreasing the activation energy of the transformation.

Step 4: Desorption and Final Answer
Once the reaction occurs and product molecules are synthesized, the bonds holding them to the metal atoms weaken, allowing the products to desorb from the catalyst surface into the fluid phase. This frees the surface active sites for a new catalytic cycle. Thus, the proper sequence is diffusion/adsorption onto active sites, bonding with metal \(d\) and \(s\) electrons, weakening of reactant bonds to form intermediates, and final desorption of products (\(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q06 - Chemical disproportionation route for potassium permanganate

questiontext.text:
In the laboratory synthesis of potassium permanganate (\(\text{KMnO}_4\)) via the chemical disproportionation method, pyrolusite (\(\text{MnO}_2\)) is converted through specific stages. Arrange these stages in the correct chronological sequence:

  1. Oxidative fusion of pyrolusite (\(\text{MnO}_2\)) with potassium hydroxide and an oxidising agent (\(\text{KNO}_3\) or \(\text{O}_2\)).
  2. Extraction of the roasted mass with water to obtain a dark green solution of potassium manganate (\(\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4\)).
  3. Acidification of the manganate(VI) solution with dilute acid or carbon dioxide to induce disproportionation.
  4. Filtration to separate precipitated manganese dioxide (\(\text{MnO}_2\)) followed by crystallisation of dark purple \(\text{KMnO}_4\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Manganese(VI) in manganate ion (\(\text{MnO}_4^{2-}\)) is thermodynamically stable only in strongly alkaline solutions. When the medium is neutralized or acidified, \(\text{Mn}^{\text{VI}}\) readily undergoes disproportionation into higher (\(\text{Mn}^{\text{VII}}\)) and lower (\(\text{Mn}^{\text{IV}}\)) oxidation states.

Step 2: Formation of Manganate(VI)
First, pyrolusite ore (\(\text{MnO}_2\)) is fused with solid \(\text{KOH}\) in the presence of air or \(\text{KNO}_3\) to yield green potassium manganate:
\[2\text{MnO}_2 + 4\text{KOH} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\]

Step 3: Extraction into Aqueous Solution
The fused product is dissolved in water to generate a strongly alkaline, intensely dark green solution containing soluble \(\text{MnO}_4^{2-}\) anions.

Step 4: Disproportionation on Acidification and Isolation
Upon acidification with dilute acid, manganate disproportionates into permanganate and solid hydrated manganese dioxide:
\[3\text{MnO}_4^{2-} + 4\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\text{MnO}_4^- + \text{MnO}_2\text{(s)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\]
The precipitated insoluble \(\text{MnO}_2\) is removed by filtration, and the resulting purple filtrate is evaporated to crystallise potassium permanganate.

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct operational sequence consists of oxidative fusion of pyrolusite, aqueous extraction of potassium manganate, acidification to trigger disproportionation, and filtration of precipitated manganese dioxide followed by crystallisation of potassium permanganate (\(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q07 - Industrial processing stages for alloy steel production

questiontext.text:
Section 4.7 describes the production of specialized steels based on transition metals. Arrange the following metallurgical operations in the correct chronological sequence for manufacturing alloy steels from iron oxides:

  1. Reduction of iron oxides with carbonaceous reducing agents to produce molten crude iron.
  2. Oxidative removal of impurities (such as silicon, phosphorus, and excess carbon) via slag formation.
  3. Addition of a precisely measured, controlled proportion of carbon to establish baseline hardness.
  4. Incorporation of specific alloying transition elements (such as \(\text{Cr}\), \(\text{Mn}\), \(\text{V}\), \(\text{W}\), or \(\text{Ni}\)) to produce desired stainless or specialized steels.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The metallurgical production of alloy steels requires converting raw iron ores into purified iron, establishing the correct carbon content, and subsequently dissolving transition metals that form solid-solution alloys due to having atomic radii within 15 percent of each other.

Step 2: Iron Oxide Reduction
The process initiates in the blast furnace with the chemical reduction of natural iron ores (primarily haematite, \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\)) by carbon monoxide and coke to obtain crude molten iron (pig iron).

Step 3: Refining and Impurity Removal
Crude iron contains substantial quantities of impurities (silicon, sulfur, phosphorus, manganese). These are oxidised in a converter and removed as slag to yield refined molten iron.

Step 4: Carbon Adjustment and Transition Metal Alloying
Controlled amounts of carbon are reintroduced to achieve the specified hardness and mechanical properties. Finally, transition metals such as chromium, manganese, tungsten, vanadium, and nickel are added to yield high-strength, corrosion-resistant alloy steels or stainless steels.

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct chronological sequence is reduction of iron oxides, oxidative refining and removal of impurities, addition of controlled carbon, and final addition of alloying transition elements (\(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_SEQUENCING_Q08 - Sequential removal of electrons during transition metal ionization

questiontext.text:
When a neutral gaseous titanium atom (\(\text{Ti}\), \(Z = 22\)) is successively ionised to form \(\text{Ti}^{4+}\), electrons are removed from specific subshells. Arrange the resulting electronic configurations in the correct chronological sequence of formation as successive electrons are removed:

  1. Formation of \(\text{Ti}^+\) with outer electronic configuration \([\text{Ar}] 3d^2 4s^1\)
  2. Formation of \(\text{Ti}^{2+}\) with outer electronic configuration \([\text{Ar}] 3d^2\)
  3. Formation of \(\text{Ti}^{3+}\) with outer electronic configuration \([\text{Ar}] 3d^1\)
  4. Formation of \(\text{Ti}^{4+}\) with closed-shell configuration \([\text{Ar}] 3d^0\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Although the \(4s\) orbital is filled before the \(3d\) orbitals in neutral ground-state transition metal atoms (Aufbau principle), upon ionisation the \(4s\) electrons penetrate less and become higher in energy than the \(3d\) electrons. Consequently, \(ns\) electrons are always lost prior to \((n-1)d\) electrons.

Step 2: Loss of the First Outer Electron
Neutral titanium has the ground-state configuration \([\text{Ar}] 3d^2 4s^2\). The first ionisation removes one outermost \(4s\) electron, producing the unipositive ion with configuration \([\text{Ar}] 3d^2 4s^1\):
\[\text{Ti} \rightarrow \text{Ti}^+ + \text{e}^-\]

Step 3: Loss of the Second Outer Electron
The second ionisation removes the remaining \(4s\) electron, yielding the dipositive ion with configuration \([\text{Ar}] 3d^2\):
\[\text{Ti}^+ \rightarrow \text{Ti}^{2+} + \text{e}^-\]

Step 4: Successive Removal of Penultimate d-Electrons and Final Answer
With no \(4s\) electrons remaining, further ionisation must remove electrons from the penultimate \(3d\) subshell. Removal of the third electron forms \(\text{Ti}^{3+}\) with configuration \([\text{Ar}] 3d^1\), and removal of the fourth electron forms \(\text{Ti}^{4+}\) with the exceptionally stable noble-gas configuration \([\text{Ar}] 3d^0\). Thus, the correct sequence of configurations generated during successive ionisation is \([\text{Ar}] 3d^2 4s^1 \rightarrow [\text{Ar}] 3d^2 \rightarrow [\text{Ar}] 3d^1 \rightarrow [\text{Ar}] 3d^0\) (\(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV}\)).
